title: TC3-18867
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: I dismiss this appeal. XXXX XXXX XXXX (Appellant) is a citizen of Uganda. 1. The Appellant fears the Government of Uganda and their security apparatus. The Appellant alleges that he is sought out by government authorities because he is a former supporter of the Democratic Party (DP) and a current supporter of the National Unity Platform (NUP) political party. He claims that he has supported various political figures financially since 2010 and that he became more actively involved with the NUP and the People Power Movement when his friend, XXXX XXXX, entered politics. He claims that he was arrested along with other opposition party supporters on XXXX XXXX, 2020, and that armed men in military trousers broke into his home on XXXX XXXX, 2021. He explains that he managed to escape and went into hiding and that he also relocated his family. He explains that an agent arranged for him to receive a Canadian travel visa and that the agent informed him that he could travel in XXXX 2022. The Appellant arrived in Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2022, and requested protection shortly thereafter. 2. The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) concluded that the Appellant is not a credible witness due to multiple inconsistencies relating to his membership in the NUP and the resulting mistreatment, and the unreliability of documentation provided to support his claim. The Appellant argues that the RPD incorrectly considered objective and personal documentary evidence that supports his claims, failed to consider his own testimony about being arrested and failed to ask him about incidents of torture that he experienced in Uganda, disregarded statements in his narrative that explain a delay in leaving Uganda, and speculated that he would not be targeted in Uganda due to his membership in the Canadian NUP chapter. 3. The determinative issue on appeal is the credibility of the claim. 4. The Appellant has not established the credibility of the basis of his claim (BOC). The Appellant's testimony about his political activities in Uganda is vague, contradictory, or unsupported by documentary evidence. Letters from witnesses in Uganda contradict his allegations about his political activities in Uganda and the circumstances allegedly leading the authorities in Uganda to pursue him. The Appellant's explanations for those inconsistencies are insufficient to overcome the credibility concerns that have been identified.
I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

The Appellant has requested that the RAD admit new evidence on appeal. The Appellant submitted new evidence requests, both at the time of perfection and after perfecting his appeal. The Appellant has also requested an oral hearing arguing that the new evidence clearly rebuts most of the RPD's findings and specifically addresses the issue of his credibility. The evidence presented by the Appellant is accepted, in part

The Appellant requested that the following be admitted as new evidence at the time of perfection. a. A Statutory Declaration from the Appellant's wife, dated XXXX XXXX, 2023, and her identification; b. A letter from a XXXX at the XXXX XXXX Clinic summarizing the Appellant's treatment, dated XXXX XXXX, 2023.

On August 15, 2023, the Appellant requested that the following be admitted as new evidence, therefore after perfection: (i) A Statutory Declaration from the Appellant's wife, dated XXXX XXXX, 2023, along with her identification; (ii) Copy of Release on Bond, issued by the Uganda Police for "XXXX XXXX XXXX", dated XXXX XXXX, 2023.

According to the Law,1 I can only accept evidence that: (iii) arose after the RPD decision; or (iv) was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or (v) that the Appellant could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before the decision. (vi) If the evidence meets one or more of these requirements, I must decide if the evidence is new, credible, and relevant before I can accept it.2 (vii) In addition, if the request to admit new evidence occurs after perfection, the RAD must also consider the documents relevance and probative value, and the new evidence that the documents bring to the appeal, and whether the Appellant could have provided the documents at the time of perfection.3

The Statutory Declaration from the Appellant's wife, dated XXXX XXXX, 2023, does not meet the requirements set out in Section 110(4) in the Immigration Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). The declaration simply repeats information stated in the Appellant's BOC. This information was available to the RPD before it submitted its decision.

The letter from the Appellant's XXXX is accepted as new evidence. It is dated XXXX XXXX, 2023, and indicates that he has been undertaking XXXX treatments since XXXX 2023, after the RPD issued its decision. This information is new because it is not part of the RPD record. I accept that the letter is credible in that it was prepared by a registered XXXX. Information related to the Appellant's state of mind is relevant to questions of credibility.

The Statutory Declaration from the Appellant's wife and the copy of the Release on Bond are not admitted as new evidence. I find that this evidence is too convenient to be credible. The Appellant's wife provided a declaration that is part of the RPD's evidence, and also a declaration that I have not admitted as on appeal because it contains no new evidence. I find that it is convenient that after allegedly being in hiding since XXXX 2021, suddenly, after the Appellant's claim was rejected, the Appellant's wife decided to return to XXXX, where she was allegedly arrested and detained in Uganda. It is more likely than not that this arrest was fabricated in order to remedy the credibility problems inherent to the Appellant's claim. On a balance of probabilities, the Appellant's wife would not return to a location where she was allegedly being told that people are regularly coming around in search of the Appellant if his claims of harm were credible. Additionally, the Release on Bond document contains credibility problems. The document's seal is not fully visible. The document is not signed by the officer who would have completed the release on bond. The document is dated XXXX XXXX, 2023, and indicates that the Appellant's wife was to appear in court on XXXX XXXX, 2023. In the Statutory Declaration dated XXXX XXXX, 2023, the Appellant's wife does not indicate that she appeared in court or failed to appear in court, for example, because she is in hiding, or whether she has been reporting to the XXXX Central station every 10 days as claimed in the declaration. The documents that are part of the late request for new evidence are not credible.

I also find that the documents that I am not accepting as new evidence do not speak to the credibility concerns raised by the RPD, which go to the heart of whether the Appellant was a member of the NUP in Uganda and the circumstances of the alleged arrest by police. These statements and documents presume that the credibility of the basis of the claim has been established and speak to the prospective risk of harm related to an ongoing interest that the Ugandan authorities would have in the Appellant. They do not serve to establish the credibility of the Appellant's political activities in Uganda and therefore they are not relevant to the primary determinative issue.
Given that I have only accepted the XXXX letter on appeal, which does not speak to the credibility issues that are determinative of the claim, it is not necessary to hold an oral hearing.
My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.4 Credibility

The RPD determined that though the Appellant alleges that he is targeted by the Ugandan government and security forces due to his membership in the NUP and his mobilization work on their behalf, he was not a member of the NUP in Uganda. It found that testimony and personal documents submitted to support his claim are inconsistent with the Appellant's Basis of Claim form (BOC) narrative.

After listening to the hearing recording and considering all of the evidence before me, I find that the Appellant has not established the basis of his claim on a balance of probabilities. The Appellant has not established his membership in the NUP, in Uganda, or his profile as a NUP mobilizer
The Appellant claims that he joined the NUP on XXXX XXXX, 2020, in XXXX, Uganda.

The RPD found that the Appellant could describe the NUP's party objective in broad terms but that his level of knowledge was not commensurate with his alleged profile as a supporter of the People Power Movement since 2017 and a party member since 2020.

The Appellant argues that the RPD did not provide clear reasons for its finding that his knowledge and engagement with the NUP was minimal. He submits that the RPD only asked a general question about the NUP "and did not make any difference and thus, clarifications between the roles in the NUP as a political party."5 He submits that he testified, in a straightforward manner, that he was mobilizing by encouraging people to register their national identity cards and vote, and to support the party and remove the dictator, indicating that he was more of a supporter and an NUP member in the field who was not attending meetings. He argues that the RPD did not ask further questions to clarify whether there were differences between members whose role was to mobilize the people and members who were within the NUP leadership structure. He argues that the RPD further erred by failing to ask further questions about the NUP's slogans while only relying upon one general slogan and that the RPD did not consider his education and personal background when assessing his knowledge of the party.

The Appellant's arguments have not persuaded me that the RPD erred. The RPD asked several questions about the Appellant's political involvement. The Appellant could not answer any detailed questions about his local NUP chapter's structure and testified that he was not able to attend any party meetings at the local chapter. The RPD asked the Appellant what is the NUP's slogan, and he could not answer that simple question, though the slogan is printed on a letter from the NUP that he submitted as part of his evidence.6 The RPD was not required to continue to ask the Appellant questions in order to coax the correct answer from him. The Appellant is a self-described important mobilizer within the NUP who is close to party leadership. Knowing the party slogan does not require any particular educational background. It was correct of the RPD to find that a party mobilizer in the field would know the party slogan. His inability to answer simple questions about the NUP calls into question the credibility of his engagement with the party and the claim that he is sought out as a political dissident.

The Appellant's connection to the NUP party and its predecessor, the People Party Movement, appears to be that he was a personal friend of an MP and of XXXX XXXX , and that he made donations as a local business owner. Contradictions in his evidence are such that he has not established that he played a larger role as a mobilizer in the field, on a balance of probabilities. The Appellant has not established that he was a member of the NUP's XXXX chapter

The Appellant provided the RPD with a letter from the NUP's XXXX chapter.7 That letter contains the Appellant's Toronto NUP membership number though he claims to have been a member of the local chapter before leaving Uganda and testified that the police confiscated his NUP XXXX chapter membership card when he was arrested. The RPD asked the Appellant why the XXXX chapter would include his Toronto membership number instead of a local chapter number to confirm his membership. The Appellant testified that the XXXX offices had been broken into and that those people stole documents and deleted information in the system. When further questioned about the break in, the Appellant admitted that he had no evidence to establish the incident and that he was speculating.

On appeal, the Appellant argues that the RPD erred because it did not take into account that the letter was coming from a third party and that he arranged for the letter to arrive through an agent. I do not accept the Appellant's argument and find that it amplifies rather than resolves the problems with the letter. His argument on appeal does not explain why he invented a break in in order to explain the problems with the letter. I find that his impulse to invent an incident to resolve a credibility concern detracts from his overall credibility. The Appellant's explanation that he arranged for the letter through an agent also detracts from its credibility because he cannot testify to how the letter was obtained from the chapter or its authenticity. His explanation that he sent them his NUP Toronto membership information so that the letter could be produced detracts from the credibility of the claim that he was previously a member of the party in Uganda. Like the RPD, I find that the Appellant's response to the RPD's concern about the NUP XXXX chapter's letter detracts from the credibility of his assertion that he was a member of the NUP in Uganda and that he is sought out in Uganda for this reason. The RPD did not err by assigning no weight to the letter.

I find that the Appellant has not established his membership in the NUP's XXXX chapter on a balance of probabilities. The XXXX chapter's letter reference to the NUP Toronto membership number and its reference to the Appellant as a foot soldier call into question its credibility. The Appellant testified that a foot soldier is one who moves on foot going door to door explaining the party's ideas and objectives, yet he was unable to recall a basic detail about the NUP's slogan. The letter refers to the Appellant as big fish of the NUP, yet he testified that he does not know who are the leaders taking the lead in the XXXX chapter, and that he was not able to attend meetings with the chairman and the MP, who recruited him to politics, because in those times, he was running up and down. I find that the Appellant's testimony contradicts the letter's characterization of his profile as a big fish. The problems with the letter, together with credibility concerns identified in other letters from alleged witnesses, cause me to conclude that he has not established the credibility of his political profile or activities in Uganda. The Appellant has not established that he was mistreated by authorities in Uganda on a balance of probabilities Letters from KS and MD
The RPD concluded that alleged mistreatment by the Ugandan government did not happen due to evidence submitted to corroborate his allegations that are inconsistent with his BOC narrative.

A letter of support from a friend, KS8, indicates that the Appellant was arrested in 2020 and tortured by the police during his detention. The Appellant's BOC omits any mention of being tortured. When asked about the omission, the Appellant responded that he only put down a brief summary in his BOC. When asked how his friend knew about the torture, the Appellant responded that his friend was arrested at the same time. When asked why his friend did not mention being arrested at the same time in his letter, the Appellant did not know why. The RPD placed low weight on the friend's letter and drew a negative inference about the omission from the Appellant's BOC.

The Appellant argues that the RPD erred because it did not ask specific questions about whether he was actually tortured or witnessed the torture of others who were arrested with him. He relies upon a statement in his friend's letter indicating that his friend "was aware" of his arrest. He adds that the objective evidence on Uganda indicates that authorities broke up opposition rallies, arrested government critics and opposition members, and placed restrictions on the media.

I do not accept the Appellant's arguments and find that the RPD correctly detracted from his credibility due to the omission from his BOC. The RPD asked the Appellant what happened when he was arrested and specifically asked him to fill in the details. The Appellant's testimony about his arrest was vague and contained very general information. For example, when asked where he was protesting, he responded in XXXX town. When asked about the particular place, the Appellant responded that he protested on the streets. When asked what happened, he testified that they arrested whomever they came across. When asked who are "they," he responded "the army people". I find this testimony to be very vague and general, and I detract from the credibility of the claim that he was arrested in XXXX 2020.

I find that his friend's statement about being aware of the Appellant's problems does not resolve the credibility concerns that the RPD raised. I agree with the RPD that the letter's credibility and probative value is diminished by the mention of torture that the Appellant did not allege in his BOC and by the omission of the friend's alleged arrest, as claimed by the Appellant in his oral testimony. These inconsistencies lead me to assign no weight to the letter. The letter is inconsistent with the Appellant's claims and the Appellant's explanations further exacerbate those inconsistencies.

The RPD found that a letter from a friend, MD9, not to be credible. In the letter, MD claims to be aware that the Appellant has been imprisoned several times and received death threats. The Appellant only alleges that he was detained once. The Appellant testified that he does not know why the letter indicates that he was imprisoned several times, and that he and MD were arrested together. When asked why MD does not indicate that he was arrested with the Appellant, the Appellant responded that he did not know why. The RPD did not find the Appellant's explanations to be reasonable and placed low weight on the letter.

On appeal, the Appellant argues that documents that corroborate some aspects of a person's story cannot be discounted merely because they do not corroborate other aspects of a story or provide sufficient detail. He submits that the RPD erred because it did not consider the Appellant's testimony that he was arrested and repeats the argument relating to objective evidence indicating that opposition members are arrested by government authorities.

While I agree that in some cases a document that corroborates some aspects of a person's story should not be discounted when it does not corroborate other aspects of the story, I find that this argument does not apply to the Appellant's documentary evidence. The problem with the letters from MD and KS is that they directly contradict the Appellant's allegations. MD's letter speaks of several imprisonments where the claim is that there was one detention. This inconsistency renders MD's claim that he is aware of the Appellant's story unreliable. MD has not corroborated the Appellant's claims with credible testimony. The Appellant's claim that he was arrested with MD and KS is not corroborated by either affiant.

I note that the letter from KS indicates that he personally involved the Appellant in politics as a mobilizer in 2010 whereas the Appellant's narrative indicates that BN approached him and requested that he support her campaign while she was a member of the Democratic Party (DP). The Appellant writes that he supported BN financially and mobilized votes for her, and continued meeting her as village mates until 2015 when she asked him to actively join politics. There is no mention in the Appellant's narrative of KS, whereas KS writes that he approached the Appellant in 2010 and that the Appellant has always supported his campaign through finances and voter mobilisation. KS also claims that he was a member of the DP with the Appellant when they were youths. The Appellant's narrative does not mention being a DP member in his youth. The Appellant testified that he joined the DP in 2017 and had dealings with that party prior to becoming a member just to help the MP, BN. The Appellant's narrative and testimony contradicts KS's testimony. I find that this is an additional reason to assign no weight to KS's letter for the purposes of corroborating the Appellant's claim.

Both KS and MD state that they are aware that the Appellant was arrested and that he fled to Canada after being threatened. However, neither affiant explained how they became aware of these facts. Given that neither affiant was able to credibly speak to the Appellant's sole alleged arrest and given that neither affiant declared being arrested along with the Appellant as he claims that they were, I find that they are not credible witnesses to the Appellant's alleged troubles.

It is for all of these reasons that I assign no weight to the letters from MD and KS with respect to establishing that the Appellant was detained by government authorities in Uganda because he is an opposition party member or because he opposes government policies or practices. Moreover, it is the Appellant who submitted letters that contradict his claims and who responded that he does not know why his affiants did or did not include relevant information in their letters, and this detracts from his own credibility.

Mentions of mistreatment of opposition members in the National Documentation Package (NDP) for Uganda do not establish the Appellant's own claims of mistreatment, on a balance of probabilities. The fact that others in Uganda have experienced problems does not establish the Appellant's own political activities on a balance of probabilities and does not do away with the contradictions and the inconsistencies in the Appellant's own claim and testimony. Other supporting documentation does not establish the basis of the claim

On appeal, the Appellant does not respond to each of the RPD's conclusions about other documentation that he submitted in support of his claim. Rather, he submits that the arguments relating to the letters from KS and MD also apply to these conclusions. I find that this argument is insufficient to overcome the concerns identified by the RPD. My own examination leads me to support the RPD's conclusion that the evidence is insufficient to establish the credibility of the basis of the claim. Additionally, I have noted the following problems with some of this evidence that add to the RPD's credibility concerns.

A letter from KI10 contains an allegation that was omitted from the Appellant's BOC. KI's letter states that many youths and members of his association were arrested, tortured and killed because of their close association with the Appellant. KI ties grave problems that other members allegedly experienced to the Appellant. The Appellant did not make this claim in his oral or written testimony. This claim is very different from the claim that youths or members of the NUP were tortured or harassed by the police because of their own political beliefs. Considering that other letters from alleged witnesses also contain allegations that are not part of the Appellant's BOC or his oral testimony, I find that this letter is not reliable, and I assign it no weight with respect to establishing or corroborating the Appellant's claim that he is sought out by government authorities in Uganda.

The Appellant alleges that he has close friendships with BN and with XXXX XXXX. He alleges that he has known BN since at least 2010 and XXXX XXXX since at least 2008. In his story, they are the main people who invite him into politics within the DP and NUP parties, and his association with them is the main reason why he is allegedly sought out in Uganda. I do not accept the Appellant's explanations that BN and XXXX XXXX are too sick or too busy to provide him with corroboration. The Appellant testified that he did not attempt to contact them for these reasons, not that he was told by them or their representatives that they could not provide him with letters. Given the contradictions and inconsistencies in his evidence, I detract from the credibility of his claim because he did not attempt to obtain corroboration from these two people. The delay in leaving Uganda detracts from the credibility of a subjective fear of harm

The Appellant argues that the RPD erred by finding that his delay of five months living in Uganda before leaving the country indicates a lack of subjective fear. He cites his BOC, indicating that an agent helped him to secure a Canadian visa but later advised him to wait while he searched for another purpose of travel and that the agent informed him only in XXXX 2022 that he can travel. He adds that his BOC indicates that he was hiding in the meantime and that workers informed him that people were coming around.

I find that the RPD correctly concluded that the Appellant's decision to remain in Uganda between receiving his travel visa in XXXX 2021 and his departure in XXXX 2022 detracts from a subjective fear of harm. While the delay alone is not determinative, the Appellant claims that he was actively sought out and that those who threaten him were visiting his home. The Appellant had a travel visa allowing him to leave Uganda immediately and did not. I do not accept the Appellant's explanation that he was later told that he could travel in XXXX 2022. His Temporary Resident Visa (TRV) application indicates that he always intended to travel in XXXX 2022.11 The Application was signed on XXXX XXXX, 2021. The XXXX 2022 travel date is indicated in a letter dated XXXX XXXX, 2021, and signed by the Appellant in a manner that is similar to how he signed his BOC application and his NUP membership card after arriving in Canada. The evidence before me indicates that the intention was always to travel in XXXX 2022, which leads me to conclude that he did not subjectively fear harm in the period of time between XXXX 2021 and XXXX 2022.

Additionally, the Appellant claims that his BOC indicates that he was hiding. His BOC indicates that he was hiding as of XXXX 2021. This claim creates an additional credibility concern related to why he remained in Uganda in hiding for more than a year despite receiving a travel visa in XXXX 2021. This inconsistency between his alleged fear and his allegations further causes me to detract from the credibility of the claim and to conclude that his behaviour is indicative of a lack of subjective fear of harm. The Appellant's mental health condition does not explain the contradictions and the inconsistencies that detract from the credibility of his claim

The Appellant submits that the RPD erred because it did not ask any questions about his mental health and condition when it started to doubt his credibility. The Appellant acknowledges that Counsel also did not raise these issues at the RPD. There was no evidence presented to the RPD suggesting that the Appellant was suffering from any mental health concerns that would affect his ability to testify. The evidence presented to the RAD on appeal also does not suggest anything that would explain the numerous credibility problems identified in the RPD's decision or in this decision. A letter from his XXXX12 indicates only that he is suffering from XXXX and XXXX without explaining how the XXXX arrived at this conclusion and without indicating how his condition could impact his testimony. This letter is insufficient to establish that mental health concerns are responsible for any inconsistencies or a lack of credible testimony. The Appellant has not established the credibility of the basis of his claim

The objective evidence on the treatment of NUP supporters does indicate that those who are politically active supporters of the NUP in Uganda can face government oppression.13 Supporters who have been targeted include the NUP's president, MPs, polling station employees, election observers, and active protesters. The contradictions identified in the RPD's decision and in this decision mean that the Appellant has not established the credibility of his claim that he had a political profile that would subject him to government oppression. He has not established that he has knowledge of the party that one might reasonably expect of an active party mobilizer. He has not credibly explained why the letter from the XXXX chapter only refers to his Toronto NUP membership number. His supporting documentation contradicts his own testimony about the nature of his political activities and his arrest in Uganda. Taken together, these contradictions cause me to conclude that he has not established his political profile on a balance of probabilities, that he was arrested in XXXX 2020 on a balance of probabilities, or that he is sought out by authorities in Uganda. Sur Place Claim

The RPD did not err in finding that the Appellant has not established the credibility of a sur place claim related to his membership in the NUP's Toronto chapter. The Appellant's appeal arguments are unclear and do not respond to the specific conclusions that the RPD made in its decision about his political participation in Canada: The panel erred when concluded that the Appellant's membership in NUP Toronto chapter was to have garnered the attention of Ugandan authorities or made him a target of the government as this finding by the panel is made on speculations, taken into account the previous statement made by the panel that in the NDP there was no evidence indicating that the Ugandan government is known for tracking NUP members in foreign jurisdictions.14

The RPD accepted that the Appellant joined the NUP's Toronto chapter in XXXX 2022 but found that given his limited implication, his membership in that chapter is insufficient to establish a serious possibility of persecution in Uganda.

I find that the RPD's determination is correct. The RPD noted that the Appellant only attended three meetings with the Toronto chapter, that he has not taken on any official responsibilities with the Toronto NUP, and that there was no evidence that he has been vocally critical of the Ugandan government or that he has been politically active on social media. The RPD correctly considered the Appellant's testimony on this issue.

I find that the RPD has correctly characterized the Appellant's political activities in Canada. I find that joining the Toronto NUP and passively attending three meetings does not establish that the Appellant has a political profile that establishes him to be an opposition critic that the Ugandan government would take note of or track in a foreign jurisdiction leading him to be targeted in Uganda.

I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
